a simple correlational analysis was applied to the crowdstorming project dataset

spans.note: restates project-level goal of comparing statistical approaches across teams
caveat about whether the simple approach is elegant or naïve

spans.assertion: player-referee dyads were excluded when the skin tone had been rated by either of the two raters
when skin tone was rated by both raters, the mean of the two ratings was used
red card proportion (relative to games played) was used instead of raw red-card frequency counts
a Spearman non-parametric correlation was used in all cases
the correlation between rated skin tone and red card proportion was small but statistically significant (Spearman's ρ=.010, d=.020)
a number of additional correlations were calculated to provide interpretational context for the small significant correlation
the skin tone/red card correlation was tested for significance separately by referee country
only referee countries yielding sufficient data, defined as more than 20 degrees of freedom, were selected for the country-level analysis
of the 161 referee countries in the dataset, only 58 had a sufficient amount of data
a Bonferroni correction was applied to the individual country-level correlations
after Bonferroni correction, none of the individual referee-country correlations were statistically significant
correlations of red card proportion with player height and weight were calculated as an additional follow-up
height and weight correlations were used as control correlations, expected not to meaningfully relate to red card likelihood
a dyad was excluded from the height/weight correlations if the player's height or weight was missing
both the height and weight correlations were statistically significant
the height and weight correlation magnitudes were nearly as large as the skin tone correlation
given the comparable magnitude to the height/weight control correlations, it is unlikely the skin-tone dyad correlation is meaningfully significant
the correlation was recalculated after collapsing the data across referee
the referee-collapsed correlation was significant and markedly larger than the player-referee dyad correlation (ρ=.051, d=.10)
the larger collapsed-across-referee correlation suggests there may be a small effect of skin tone on red card issuance
for the secondary research question, a correlation between skin tone and red card proportion was calculated incorporating implicit and explicit racial attitudes
partial correlation and multiplicative approaches were used to test for an influence of racial attitudes
none of the racial-attitude correlations yielded meaningful relationships (all ρ<.02, d≈.02)
the feedback provided did not notably influence the analytical approach

spans.note: describes a reviewer comment suggesting player position be incorporated

spans.assertion: the analysis was re-run with referee collapsed out, which was the analysis producing the largest effect size (d=.10)
players were divided into four position categories: back, midfielder, forward/winger, and goalkeeper
players whose position was not available were excluded from the position follow-up analysis
the skin tone/red card correlation was re-calculated after excluding players with unavailable position data
after that exclusion, the effect was found to be slightly stronger (ρ=.062, p=.020, d=.12)
the position-specific correlations were corrected for multiple comparisons
none of the position-specific correlations were significant after that correction

for all positions other than goalkeeper, correlations were similar to each other but higher than the overall estimate (ρ between .086–.117, d between .17–.23), attributed to removing position-related variability
the correlation was negative for the goalkeeper position
results from the simple correlational approach show no meaningful effect of skin tone on issuance of red cards (restated as conclusion)
